title: Adding the April-March temperature difference reduced later leaf-date gap errors in two German regions in 1991-2020
abstract: We tested a Swiss result in a separate German observation network. We used 45,356 paired birch and beech leaf dates at 1,093 stations in 1961-2020. Models controlled station means, winter and mean spring temperature, and time. The April-minus-March gap slopes were negative in all four region-period samples. Three family intervals were below zero; the early northern interval included zero. Frozen 1961-1990 models with the monthly difference reduced 1991-2020 root mean square error by 2.57 percent in the North and 6.55 percent in the South. Conditional two-region family intervals were 1.53-3.93 and 3.81-9.94 percent. Added year effects gave clear local support only in the later North. Early pair availability was linked to the temperature difference. Seven-day species-specific reporting delays permit either point-slope sign in all four samples. Thus the test gives partial support for using the monthly difference in later estimates with known weather. It does not establish a stable causal response, accurate event dates, or ecological harm. Raw sources and record tables stay external. The package gives original code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, figures and exact reproduction steps.

display.caption: Left: April-minus-March slopes of the beech-minus-birch date gap. Bars are four-test family intervals from annual-score HAC errors. Right: later-year error reduction for the added term. Bars are two-region family block intervals conditional on frozen training fits and retained stations. A negative slope is not proof of a shorter absolute gap or a causal effect.
Point slopes in all planned checks. Year effects leave only spatial weather differences within years. These point estimates do not replace the intervals in results.csv. Regions share weather.

citations.reason: A new German observation-network test of its birch-beech monthly contrast and later-year error gain. We use the same weather product, but no Swiss biological records or prior code.
Prior Swiss seasonal-contrast and leaf-span evidence. The species set and observation network differ.
Prior German and Swiss single-species thermal-time test defines competing explanations. Some German biological records overlap.
Related German paired oak-beech null result and year-effect caution. It uses a different species gap but overlapping beech records.
Related Swiss reporting-delay audit. Our outcome is the signed date gap in a separate national network, not binary order.
